A monarchist is a person who believes that a country should be ruled — or at least headed — by a monarch: a king, queen, emperor, or empress. A monarchist either supports an existing monarchy or wants a monarchy to be established (or restored) in their country.

That's the heart of it. But to truly understand this word, you need to understand a few layers around it.

Before you can understand "monarchist," you need to be clear on "monarchy."

A monarchy is a system of government where a single person — called a monarch — holds the title of head of state, usually for life, and usually because they were born into a royal family. The position is most commonly passed down from parent to child. This is called hereditary succession — meaning you don't vote for a king or queen; they inherit the role by birth.

Examples of monarchies today include the United Kingdom (King Charles III), Spain (King Felipe VI), Japan (Emperor Naruhito), Saudi Arabia, Sweden, Norway, and Denmark, among others.

The opposite of a monarchy is a republic, where the head of state is typically elected by the people (like a president).
Step 2: So What Exactly Does a Monarchist Believe?

A monarchist is someone who thinks monarchy is good, right, legitimate, or the best option for a country. Here is what that can mean in practice:

  • They may believe a monarch gives a country stability and continuity — a royal family provides a constant, non-political symbol of national identity that doesn't change with every election.
  • They may believe monarchy is historically legitimate — that certain royal families have a rightful, centuries-long claim to rule their nation.
  • They may believe monarchy strengthens national tradition, culture, and pride.
  • They may hold religious views — for example, some monarchists believe that kings and queens are chosen or blessed by God, giving their rule a divine legitimacy.
  • They may simply believe that a monarchy, especially a modern constitutional one, works well in practice.

A monarchist doesn't necessarily think the monarch should have unlimited power. They just believe the institution of monarchy itself should exist and be preserved or restored.
Step 3: The Two Broad Types of Monarchists

Not all monarchists believe the same thing. There are two major varieties:

1. Absolute Monarchists

These are monarchists who believe the monarch should have full, unrestricted power over the country — the ability to make laws, command armies, and rule without needing the approval of a parliament or the public. This was the dominant form of monarchy in Europe during the 1600s and 1700s. Today, absolute monarchists are rare.

2. Constitutional Monarchists

These are monarchists who believe the monarch should exist within a constitutional framework — meaning the king or queen is a symbolic or ceremonial head of state, while an elected parliament or government holds the real political power. This is by far the most common position among monarchists today.

For example, a British person who supports keeping King Charles III as head of state — even though he doesn't make laws or run the government — is a constitutional monarchist.
Step 4: A Monarchist Doesn't Have to Live in a Monarchy

This is an important nuance. A monarchist can be:

  • Someone living under a monarchy who supports and wants to keep it (e.g., a British person who defends the Royal Family).
  • Someone living in a republic who wishes their country had a monarchy or wants to restore a monarchy that was abolished in the past.

For example, France abolished its monarchy during the French Revolution in the late 1700s. Even today, there are French citizens who believe the French royal family (the Bourbon or Orléans dynasties) should be restored to power. These people are called French monarchists.

Similarly, after Russia's Tsar Nicholas II was overthrown and killed during the Russian Revolution (1917), many Russians who fled abroad remained monarchists — hoping the imperial family would one day be restored to the throne.
Step 5: What is a Monarchist Opposed To?

Understanding what a monarchist stands against helps sharpen the meaning:

  • Republicans (in the political science sense, not the American party): People who believe in a republic — that heads of state should be elected, not born into the role. A republican and a monarchist are on opposite sides of this debate.
  • Abolitionists (in the context of monarchy): People who want to completely end or abolish the monarchy in their country.
  • Revolutionaries: Historically, monarchists were often opposed to political revolutions that sought to overthrow royal rule and replace it with elected governments or republics.
Step 6: How the Word Is Used in Real Life

The word "monarchist" appears most often in:

Historical contexts:

  • "After the French Revolution, many monarchists fled to Austria and Prussia, hoping to overthrow the new republic and restore the king."
  • "The English Civil War of the 1640s was a conflict between monarchists (who supported King Charles I) and parliamentarians (who believed Parliament should hold power)."

Modern political contexts:

  • "The debate over whether Australia should become a republic continues to divide monarchists and republicans in that country."
  • "He is a committed monarchist who believes the British Crown is essential to national identity."

Descriptive contexts:

  • A political party, a newspaper, a thinker, or a movement can all be described as "monarchist" if they advocate for monarchy.

Since you want to fully understand this word, here are closely related terms you'll see used alongside it:

  • Monarchy — the system of government a monarchist supports.
  • Monarchism — the ideology or belief system itself (the "-ism" form).
  • Monarchical — the adjective form, meaning "relating to or characteristic of a monarchy" (e.g., "monarchical tradition").
  • Royalist — a very similar word to monarchist; often used interchangeably, though "royalist" can carry a stronger emotional loyalty to a specific royal family, while "monarchist" is broader and more ideological.
  • Anti-monarchist — a person who opposes monarchy.
  • Republican (political science sense) — a person who supports a republic over a monarchy.

A monarchist is a person who believes that a country should have — or keep — a monarch (a king, queen, or emperor) as its head of state, whether because of tradition, stability, legitimacy, religion, or simply because they think it works well for society.
